title: 2.2 Anatomical Planes and Major Body Movements

cards.front: How is a person oriented in the standard anatomical position, and why is this standardized posture essential in biomechanics?
cards.back:
In the standard anatomical position:
  • The body is standing erect.
  • The arms are resting down at the sides.
  • The palms face forward (supinated).
This universal orientation serves as the neutral starting reference for describing all planes, axes, joint articulations, and directional terms, eliminating ambiguity during movement analysis.

cards.front: Define the three cardinal anatomical planes of the human body and describe how each plane sections bodily structures.
cards.back:
The body is sliced across three mutually perpendicular cardinal planes:
  • Sagittal Plane: Slices the body vertically into left and right sections (not necessarily at the midline).
  • Frontal (Coronal) Plane: Slices the body vertically into front and back (anterior and posterior) sections.
  • Transverse (Horizontal) Plane: Slices the body horizontally into upper and lower (superior and inferior) sections.
Clinical Reference: Anatomical views in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are standardly aligned with these three planes.

cards.front: What primary joint actions and resistance exercise movements occur within the sagittal plane?
cards.back:
Movements parallel to the sagittal plane consist primarily of forward and backward actions:
  • Primary Joint Actions: Flexion (decreasing joint angle) and extension (increasing joint angle).
  • Resistance Exercise Example: The standing barbell curl (elbow flexion and extension), as well as back squats, lunges, and linear running strides.

cards.front: What primary joint actions and resistance exercise movements occur within the frontal plane?
cards.back:
Movements parallel to the frontal plane consist of side-to-side, lateral actions:
  • Primary Joint Actions: Abduction (moving away from the midline), adduction (moving toward the midline), lateral spinal flexion, and ankle inversion/eversion.
  • Resistance Exercise Example: The standing lateral dumbbell raise (shoulder abduction and adduction), as well as lateral lunges and side shuffles.

cards.front: What primary joint actions and resistance exercise movements occur within the transverse plane?
cards.back:
Movements parallel to the transverse plane involve rotational actions and horizontal limb motions:
  • Primary Joint Actions: Internal (medial) rotation, external (lateral) rotation, horizontal adduction, horizontal abduction, and axial torso rotation.
  • Resistance Exercise Example: The dumbbell fly (horizontal adduction and abduction at the glenohumeral joint), seated cable twists, and batting/swinging motions.

cards.front: In the absence of specialized biomechanical laboratory equipment, what practical method is adequate for analyzing sport movements, and what technologies facilitate it?
cards.back:
In the absence of specialized equipment and technical expertise, simple visual observation is fully adequate for identifying the primary kinematic features of a sport movement.

Coaches can enhance observational accuracy using:
  • Slow-Motion Videotape / High-Speed Video: Slows rapid athletic actions to eliminate motion blur and facilitate observation of joint sequencing.
  • Commercially Available Software: Digital motion analysis apps that allow frame-by-frame scrubbing, joint angle measurements, and kinematic tracking.

cards.tag: Specificity of Training via Joint Kinematics
cards.front: How does qualitative biomechanical observation directly guide exercise selection under the principle of specificity of training?
cards.back:
Through visual observation or video analysis, the strength and conditioning professional identifies the target sport activity's primary joint actions and planes of motion.

Under the specificity of training principle, exercises are selected that involve similar movement around the same joints, ensuring mechanical and neuromuscular transfer to competition.

cards.front: Why is exercise prescription based on the three cardinal planes effective even though few athletic movements occur purely in a single plane?
cards.back:
Although few real-world athletic movements occur exclusively in one cardinal plane (most sport skills are diagonal, multi-planar, or spiral), there is sufficient overlap of training effects.

Exercising muscles systematically within the three major cardinal planes also strengthens and stabilizes them for complex, diagonal movements occurring between the planes.

cards.front: Which lower-body and torso sport movements are commonly omitted from standard resistance training programs, and what sports demand them?
cards.back:
Standard programs often overemphasize bilateral sagittal lifting, neglecting:
  • Knee Flexion: Vital in sprinting (hamstring recovery mechanics).
  • Hip Flexion: Critical in sprinting knee drive and kicking.
  • Ankle Dorsiflexion: Essential in running ground strikes and tibial stress management.
  • Hip Internal and External Rotation: Required for pivoting and dynamic change of direction.
  • Hip Adduction and Abduction: Essential for lateral cutting maneuvers and pelvic stability.
  • Torso Rotation: Fundamental for rotational power in throwing and batting.

cards.front: Which upper-body and cervical movements are frequently omitted from standard resistance programs, and what sports require them?
cards.back:
Critical movements often omitted from standard training include:
  • Shoulder Internal and External Rotation: Critical in throwing (baseball, football) and tennis for rotator cuff acceleration and eccentric deceleration of the arm.
  • Neck Movements (Flexion, Extension, Lateral Flexion, Rotation): Essential in boxing and wrestling to develop cervical muscular stiffness, dissipate impact forces, and protect against head and neck injury.
